rv.q: It is thrilling and essential theater that interrogates the present by laying bare how history is written.

It’s also fair to see, without giving away a truly disturbing ending, that The Minutes lifts itself from a satire of mundane corruption and small-town secrecy to something like an indictment of the very notion of America’s self-perception.
It makes for an ugly and shocking — but also wholly appropriate — adjournment to an electrifying meeting with America’s shame.
It’s an important play, a visceral theatrical experience, all about what has happened to retail American democracy and how this nation decides on which stories about itself it wants to believe.
For long stretches, The Minutes, is dull, which Letts seems to intend as a feature, not a bug.
Mr. Letts delivers it with the skill of a master dramatist who knows that the most effective horror is the kind that emerges from the most ordinary circumstances.
Adding to the old-hat vibe, the controversial final moment (one queasy woman ran out of the theater) believes that it’s bolder and more thought-provoking than it really is.
Instead of truly reckoning with that bloody legacy, Letts chooses to pull his punches.
The play shakes and starts to fly to pieces, a Superleggera car taken off-road.
One thing is clear, if there is one play you choose to see on Broadway this season, have it be The Minutes.
It’s the kind of serious work that provokes passionate debate and will linger in your memory.
The cast, a starry ensemble, deliciously captures the pettiness, pomposity, self-dealing and general surreal lunacy of local politicos
It does not detonate the play but feels like a sledgehammer just took the place of a fine chisel.
Tracy Letts’ The Minutes is both a fine political comedy as well as an indictment of how most Americans live today.

Perhaps it is this civil discourse that Letts was inspired to explore and dismantle — a reminder that theater has the power to, if not transform, at least question the beliefs we've come to assume are facts.
Letts is workmanlike as an actor and bold as a playwright, taking a risk on an unsettling ending that is out of harmony with its build up.
It is a stunning crash landing for an otherwise very good play.
You may find yourself always about 30 minutes ahead of what’s happening in “The Minutes,” which is a problem for a play that lasts only 90.
If a town reflects its residents, this place is wormy all the way down to its stony pit.
The feeling, regrettably, is mutual.
The Minutes is a piece as mysterious as it is ferociously entertaining.

cn.t: Critics find Letts' dark civic satire starts as amusing small-town comedy before taking a disturbing turn into America's revisionist history. The strong ensemble and sharp dialogue earn praise, though some find the ending heavy-handed.
